module_title: Types of Pesticides and How They Work

lessons.title: Contact vs. Systemic Pesticides: What Works Best
lessons.body: When you spray a pesticide, it either stays on the surface where it lands (contact) or gets absorbed into the plant and moves inside it (systemic). Knowing the difference saves you money and gets better pest control. Contact pesticides kill pests only when they are hit directly by the spray. They work fast but have no residual effect. Examples include pyrethroids like deltamethrin and organophosphates like malathion. These are good for pests that sit on the outside of leaves, like aphids or beetles. But if the pest hides under the leaf or inside the stem, contact sprays miss them. Systemic pesticides are absorbed by leaves or roots and travel through the plant's vascular system. Pests die when they feed on any part of the plant. Examples include imidacloprid and thiamethoxam. These are excellent for sap-sucking pests like whiteflies, mealybugs, and stem borers. In Africa, systemic pesticides are popular for cotton, maize, and vegetables because they protect new growth. However, systemic pesticides can harm pollinators if used on flowering crops. Always check the label for bee warnings. For best results, match the pesticide type to the pest's behaviour. If pests feed openly, contact sprays work. If they hide, use systemic. Also consider cost: contact pesticides are usually cheaper, but systemic ones last longer. In smallholder farms, knapsack sprayers are common. With contact pesticides, you must spray the undersides of leaves thoroughly. With systemics, you can spray the whole plant and the chemical will move. Remember, no pesticide works if the pest isn't there. Scout your field first. Use a hand lens to check for eggs, larvae, or adults. Then choose the right type. Always wear protective gear and follow label instructions.

lessons.title: Selective vs. Non-Selective Herbicides
lessons.body: Herbicides are chemicals that kill weeds. Selective herbicides kill only certain types of plants, while non-selective herbicides kill almost all plants they touch. Choosing the right one is critical for your crop. Selective herbicides are designed to kill weeds without harming your crop. For example, 2,4-D kills broadleaf weeds in maize and wheat but does not harm the grass-like maize. Atrazine is another selective herbicide used in maize to control broadleaf and some grass weeds. These work because crops can break down the chemical while weeds cannot. Non-selective herbicides, like glyphosate and paraquat, kill any plant they contact. They are used for land clearing, pre-planting, or directed spraying between crop rows. Glyphosate is systemic and kills the whole plant including roots. Paraquat is contact and burns down foliage quickly. In Africa, non-selective herbicides are often used to clear fields before planting or to control weeds in orchards. But be careful: drift from non-selective herbicides can damage your crop if it lands on leaves. Always spray on a calm day and use a shield if needed. Selective herbicides are safer for crops but may not kill all weed species. You may need a mix or a sequence. For example, in maize, you might use atrazine early and then a grass-specific herbicide like nicosulfuron later. Read the label to see which weeds are controlled. Also, rotate herbicides with different modes of action to prevent resistance. Weeds like pigweed have developed resistance to glyphosate in many countries. If you use the same herbicide every year, resistant weeds will take over. Always calibrate your sprayer to apply the correct dose. Too little won't kill weeds; too much wastes money and can harm the crop. For smallholder farmers, hand weeding is still common, but herbicides save labour. Use selective herbicides when your crop is growing and non-selective ones only before planting or with a shield.

lessons.title: Understanding Active Ingredients and Formulations
lessons.body: Every pesticide product has two main parts: the active ingredient (AI) and the formulation. The AI is the chemical that actually kills the pest. The formulation is everything elseâsolvents, emulsifiers, carriersâthat makes the AI easy to mix, spray, and stick to surfaces. Understanding this helps you choose the right product and use it safely. Active ingredients have common names (like glyphosate) and trade names (like Roundup). The same AI can be sold under many trade names. Always look for the AI on the label. The concentration of AI is given as a percentage or grams per litre. For example, a product might say '480 g/L glyphosate' or '50% WP' (wettable powder). This tells you how much actual chemical is in the container. Formulations come in different types. Emulsifiable concentrates (EC) are liquids that mix with water to form an emulsion. They are easy to handle but can be harmful to skin. Wettable powders (WP) are dry powders that mix with water. They need constant agitation because they settle. Suspension concentrates (SC) are thick liquids that form a suspension. They are safer and easy to pour. Granules (G) are solid particles applied directly to soil. They release slowly. Each formulation affects how you spray. ECs and SCs are good for foliar sprays. WPs can clog nozzles if not mixed well. Granules are used for soil pests. In Africa, common formulations include ECs like cypermethrin 10% EC and WPs like mancozeb 80% WP. Always check the expiry date. Expired pesticides may not work or can become more toxic. Store pesticides in a cool, dry place away from children and animals. When mixing, use the correct dose. For example, if the label says 2 ml per litre, measure with a syringe or measuring cup. Never use more than recommended. Overdosing wastes money and can harm your crop. Also, some formulations require adjuvants like stickers or spreaders to improve coverage. These are added to the spray tank. Read the label for specific instructions. Understanding AIs and formulations helps you compare products and get the best value.

lessons.title: Common Active Ingredients in African Markets
lessons.body: African farmers have access to a wide range of active ingredients, but some are more common than others. Knowing these helps you choose effective and affordable pesticides. Here are the most frequently used AIs in African agriculture. For insecticides, pyrethroids like cypermethrin, deltamethrin, and lambda-cyhalothrin are widely available. They are contact insecticides that kill a broad range of pests including aphids, caterpillars, and beetles. They are cheap but can harm beneficial insects. Organophosphates like malathion and chlorpyrifos are also common, especially for stored grain pests. However, chlorpyrifos is banned in some countries due to health risks. Neonicotinoids like imidacloprid and thiamethoxam are systemic and used for sucking pests. They are popular in cotton and vegetables but are toxic to bees. For fungicides, mancozeb and copper-based products (like copper oxychloride) are staples for diseases like late blight in tomatoes and downy mildew in grapes. Mancozeb is a protectant fungicide, meaning it must be applied before disease starts. Systemic fungicides like metalaxyl and triadimefon are also available. For herbicides, glyphosate is the most common non-selective herbicide. Atrazine is widely used in maize. 2,4-D is used for broadleaf weeds in cereals. Paraquat is still used in some areas but is highly toxic and restricted in many countries. For storage pests, phosphine fumigants (like aluminium phosphide tablets) are common. They are dangerous and require professional handling. When buying pesticides, always check for the registration number from your national regulatory authority. In Kenya, look for PCPB registration. In Nigeria, NAFDAC. In South Africa, DALRRD. Avoid buying unregistered or repackaged products. They may be fake or expired. Also, consider the pre-harvest interval (PHI) â the time you must wait after spraying before harvesting. For example, cypermethrin has a PHI of 7 days on many vegetables. Always follow the label. If you cannot find a specific AI, ask an extension officer for alternatives. Rotate AIs with different modes of action to prevent resistance. For example, alternate between a pyrethroid and a neonicotinoid for aphid control. This keeps pests guessing and preserves the effectiveness of your chemicals.

lessons.title: Reading Pesticide Labels and Safety Data Sheets
lessons.body: Pesticide labels are legal documents. They tell you how to use the product safely and effectively. Ignoring them can lead to crop damage, health problems, or legal trouble. Every label has key sections you must read before buying or using. First, look for the product name and active ingredient. The active ingredient is the chemical that kills the pest. The label also lists the concentration, like '480 g/L glyphosate'. Next, check the signal word: 'DANGER' means highly toxic, 'WARNING' means moderately toxic, and 'CAUTION' means slightly toxic. In Africa, you may also see a skull and crossbones for highly toxic products. The label tells you what pests or weeds the product controls. It also gives the dose rate, like '2 ml per litre of water' or '1 kg per hectare'. Follow this exactly. Using more can harm your crop and leave residues. Using less may not work. The label also states the pre-harvest interval (PHI) â the number of days you must wait after spraying before you can harvest and eat the crop. For example, if the PHI is 14 days, do not harvest before then. The label also lists safety precautions: wear gloves, goggles, and a mask. Avoid spraying on windy days. Do not eat, drink, or smoke while spraying. Store the pesticide in its original container, locked away from children and animals. Never store pesticides in food or drink bottles. The Safety Data Sheet (SDS) is a more detailed document. It gives information on toxicity, first aid, firefighting, and spill cleanup. You can request an SDS from the seller or manufacturer. In case of poisoning, the SDS tells you what to do. For example, if someone swallows a pesticide, the SDS may say to induce vomiting or not, depending on the chemical. Always keep the label and SDS handy. If you don't understand something, ask an extension officer. Many African governments require labels in local languages or English. If the label is only in a foreign language, ask for a translation. Remember, the label is there to protect you and your crop. Read it every time, even if you have used the product before.

lessons.title: Modes of Action: How Pesticides Kill Pests
lessons.body: Modes of action (MoA) describe how a pesticide kills a pest. Knowing MoA helps you choose the right product and prevent resistance. Pesticides work in different ways, targeting specific systems in the pest. For insecticides, common MoA groups include nerve poisons, muscle poisons, and growth regulators. Pyrethroids and organophosphates attack the nervous system. They cause paralysis and death. Neonicotinoids block nerve signals, leading to paralysis. These are systemic and affect sucking pests. Insect growth regulators (IGRs) like methoprene disrupt the pest's ability to molt or reproduce. They are slow-acting but very targeted. For fungicides, MoA includes respiration inhibitors, sterol biosynthesis inhibitors, and multi-site inhibitors. For example, strobilurins (like azoxystrobin) block respiration in fungal cells. Triazoles (like tebuconazole) inhibit sterol production, weakening the fungal membrane. Multi-site inhibitors like mancozeb attack many sites, making resistance less likely. For herbicides, MoA includes photosynthesis inhibitors, amino acid synthesis inhibitors, and cell membrane disruptors. Atrazine inhibits photosynthesis. Glyphosate inhibits an enzyme (EPSPS) needed for amino acid production. Paraquat disrupts cell membranes. Weeds die because they cannot produce energy or build proteins. Resistance happens when pests survive a pesticide application and reproduce. If you use the same MoA repeatedly, resistant individuals become dominant. To prevent resistance, rotate pesticides with different MoA groups. For example, alternate between a pyrethroid (MoA group 3) and a neonicotinoid (group 4A) for aphid control. Also, use non-chemical methods like crop rotation, biological control, and hand picking. The Insecticide Resistance Action Committee (IRAC) and Herbicide Resistance Action Committee (HRAC) publish MoA classification lists. You can find them online or from extension officers. In Africa, resistance is a growing problem. For example, fall armyworm has developed resistance to some pyrethroids. By rotating MoA, you can keep your pesticides effective. Always read the label to find the MoA group. Many labels now include a group number. Use this to plan your rotation. Remember, no pesticide works forever if used alone. Integrated pest management (IPM) combines MoA rotation with other tactics for long-term control.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between contact and systemic pesticides?
options: A) Contact pesticides are absorbed by plants; systemic pesticides stay on the surface.
B) Contact pesticides kill pests only when hit directly; systemic pesticides are absorbed and move within the plant.
C) Contact pesticides are always more toxic than systemic pesticides.
D) Systemic pesticides only work on soil pests.
quiz.explanation: Contact pesticides require direct contact with the pest, while systemic pesticides are taken up by the plant and transported internally.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a systemic insecticide?
quiz.explanation: Imidacloprid is a neonicotinoid that is absorbed by plants and moves systemically.

quiz.q: When would you choose a contact pesticide over a systemic one?
options: A) When pests hide inside plant stems
B) When pests feed openly on leaves
C) When you want long-lasting protection
quiz.explanation: Contact pesticides are effective for pests that are exposed on plant surfaces.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of selective herbicides?
options: A) They kill all plants including crops.
B) They only kill specific weeds without harming the crop.
C) They are always cheaper than non-selective herbicides.
D) They do not require any safety precautions.
quiz.explanation: Selective herbicides target certain weed species while leaving the crop unharmed.

quiz.q: Which herbicide is non-selective and kills almost all plants?
quiz.explanation: Glyphosate is a non-selective systemic herbicide that kills a wide range of plants.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a formulation in a pesticide product?
options: A) To increase the toxicity of the active ingredient
B) To make the active ingredient easier to mix, spray, and stick to surfaces
C) To replace the active ingredient
D) To make the pesticide more expensive
quiz.explanation: Formulations include solvents and carriers that improve handling, mixing, and application of the active ingredient.

quiz.q: What does 'EC' stand for in pesticide formulations?
quiz.explanation: EC is Emulsifiable Concentrate, a liquid formulation that mixes with water to form an emulsion.

quiz.q: Which formulation type requires constant agitation because it settles?
quiz.explanation: Wettable powders settle quickly and need agitation to stay mixed in the spray tank.

quiz.q: Which active ingredient is commonly used as a non-selective herbicide in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Glyphosate is widely used as a non-selective herbicide for land clearing and weed control.

quiz.q: What is the pre-harvest interval (PHI)?
options: A) The time between spraying and when you can harvest safely
B) The time between mixing and spraying
C) The time between buying and using the pesticide
D) The time between two spray applications
quiz.explanation: PHI is the waiting period after pesticide application before harvesting to ensure residues are within safe limits.

quiz.q: Which regulatory body registers pesticides in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: The Pest Control Products Board (PCPB) is responsible for pesticide registration in Kenya.

quiz.q: Why is it important to rotate pesticides with different modes of action?
options: C) To make pesticides more toxic
quiz.explanation: Rotating modes of action reduces the chance that pests will develop resistance to a single chemical group.

quiz.q: What does the signal word 'DANGER' on a pesticide label indicate?
options: A) The product is slightly toxic
B) The product is moderately toxic
C) The product is highly toxic
D) The product is safe to use without protection
quiz.explanation: DANGER indicates a highly toxic product that requires strict safety precautions.

quiz.q: What is a Safety Data Sheet (SDS)?
options: A) A document that provides detailed safety and toxicity information
B) A label that tells you how to mix the pesticide
C) A receipt for your purchase
D) A list of pests controlled by the pesticide
quiz.explanation: An SDS provides comprehensive information on hazards, first aid, and safe handling of the chemical.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a nerve poison insecticide?
quiz.explanation: Cypermethrin is a pyrethroid insecticide that attacks the insect nervous system.

quiz.q: What is the mode of action of glyphosate?
quiz.explanation: Glyphosate inhibits the EPSPS enzyme, blocking amino acid production in plants.

quiz.q: Which of these is a multi-site fungicide, making resistance less likely?
quiz.explanation: Mancozeb attacks multiple sites in fungal cells, reducing the risk of resistance development.

quiz.q: What should you do if you don't understand the label instructions?
options: B) Ask an extension officer for help
C) Use double the dose to be safe
D) Ignore the label and use your own method
quiz.explanation: Extension officers can explain label instructions and ensure safe and effective use.

quiz.q: Which formulation is best for soil pests?
quiz.explanation: Granules are solid particles applied to soil, where they release the active ingredient slowly.

quiz.q: What is the first thing you should do before buying a pesticide?
options: B) Read the label and identify the active ingredient
C) Ask a friend for advice
quiz.explanation: Reading the label ensures you buy the correct product for your pest problem and understand its safe use.

quiz.q: Which of these is a selective herbicide for broadleaf weeds in maize?
quiz.explanation: 2,4-D is a selective herbicide that kills broadleaf weeds without harming grass crops like maize.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid spraying on a windy day?
options: A) The pesticide will evaporate faster
B) The spray may drift and damage non-target plants
C) The pesticide will be less effective
quiz.explanation: Wind can carry pesticide droplets to nearby crops or areas, causing unintended damage.

quiz.q: What is the role of an adjuvant in a spray tank?
options: A) To increase the toxicity of the active ingredient
B) To improve coverage and sticking of the spray
C) To replace the active ingredient
D) To make the spray dry faster
quiz.explanation: Adjuvants like stickers and spreaders help the pesticide cover and adhere to plant surfaces better.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common neonicotinoid insecticide?
quiz.explanation: Thiamethoxam is a neonicotinoid that acts systemically against sucking pests.

quiz.q: What does the acronym IRAC stand for?
options: A) International Regulatory Agency for Chemicals
D) International Research on Agricultural Chemicals
quiz.explanation: IRAC is the Insecticide Resistance Action Committee, which provides guidance on mode of action classification.

quiz.q: Which of these is a pre-planting non-selective herbicide?
quiz.explanation: Paraquat is a non-selective contact herbicide used to burn down weeds before planting.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to store pesticides in food or drink bottles?
options: A) The pesticide may lose potency
B) Someone may accidentally eat or drink it
D) The pesticide may become more toxic
quiz.explanation: Storing pesticides in food containers can lead to accidental poisoning, especially of children.

quiz.q: What is the mode of action of atrazine?
quiz.explanation: Atrazine inhibits photosynthesis in susceptible plants, leading to their death.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a protectant fungicide that must be applied before disease starts?
quiz.explanation: Mancozeb is a protectant fungicide that forms a barrier on plant surfaces before infection occurs.

quiz.q: What is the best way to prevent resistance to pesticides?
options: A) Use the same pesticide every time
B) Rotate pesticides with different modes of action
quiz.explanation: Rotating modes of action prevents pests from adapting to a single chemical group.
